chunks: Abu Ali Al-Ash'ari, from Muhammad ibn Abd al-Jabbar, from Abu Muhammad Al-Hudhali, from Ibrahim ibn Khalid Al-Qattan, from Muhammad ibn Mansur Al-Sayqal, from his father, who said:

I complained to Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) about a grief I felt for a son of mine who had died, to the extent that I feared for my mind. He said: 'If something from this hits you, let your tears flow, for it will bring you relief.'

key_terms.يَسْكُن: To calm, settle, or bring relief

ai.seo_question: What is the Islamic perspective on crying and expressing grief for the deceased?
ai.summary: In this hadith from *Al-Kafi*, the narrator Ibn al-Sayqal expresses profound grief (*wajd*) over his son's death, fearing it impaired his intellect. Imam al-Sadiq (peace be upon him) advises him to let his tears flow freely, validating emotional expression as a divinely sanctioned means of soothing the heart. This narration underscores the Shia scholarly view that grief is not a weakness but a natural state, and that weeping serves as a spiritual and psychological remedy to restore balance.

en.hubeali: Abu Ali Al Ashary, from Muhammad Bin Abdul Jabbar, from Abu Muhammad Al Huzaly, from Ibrahim Bin Khalid Al Qattan, from Muhammad Bin Mansour Al Sayqal, from his father who said,

‘I complained to Abu Abdullah<sup>asws</sup> of grief which I found to be in upon the death of a son of mine, to the extent that I feared upon my mind. So he<sup>asws</sup> said: ‘If something from this hits you, allow your tears to flow for it would you give you relief’.
en.sarwar: 3. Abu Ali al-Ash’ariy has narrated from Muhammad ibn ‘Abd Jabbar from abu Muhammad al-Hudhaliy from Ibrahim ibn Khalid al- Qattan from Muhammad ibn Mansur al-Sayqal from his father who has said the following:

“I complained before abu ‘Abd Allah, ‘Alayhi al-Salam, about feeling extremely sad for the death of my son and I feared for my sanity. He said, ‘When something like this happens, allow your tears to flow; it gives you relief.’”
